read: full: abstract, sections 1-5 (p.1-9), Appendix A (curriculum, template creation, translation, p.14-16) and E (robustness of the step-level judge, p.24-25); Appendix B-D (variant examples, prompts, extra results) and the references skimmed.
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2606.08034v2 [cs.CV], 26 September 2026, page header 'Preprint' (p.1); no venue shown.
what_it_is: Sci-rho is a symbolic, visually grounded benchmark of school-level STEM problems (Cambridge IGCSE and A-Level topics) in mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and computer science (p.1, p.3). Eight contributors (STEM graduates, advanced undergraduates, olympiad medalists) wrote 606 problems as Python classes. Each class draws its own image, samples variables from a predetermined seed, computes the answer and emits step-by-step LaTeX solutions (p.4, p.15-16). The descriptions were machine-translated into six more languages and checked by native speakers, giving 4,242 language-specific templates and, at 10 variants each, 42,420 instances (p.1, p.4-5). Seventeen VLMs are scored on average-case and worst-case accuracy across variants, with answers matched within 1% and no model involved. For five models, step precision, recall and F1 against the gold steps are judged by GPT-5.4 (p.5-7, p.24).
domain: school-level STEM (IGCSE and A-Level): mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science; multimodal; seven languages. Not engineering.
size: 606 distinct templates (Mathematics 199, Physics 195, Chemistry 137, Computer Science 52, Biology 23) x 7 languages = 4,242 templates; 10 variants each = 42,420 instances (p.1, p.5). 17 VLMs evaluated; step-level evaluation on 5 of them (p.5, p.7).
source_of_items: generated from templates: problems adapted mostly from Cambridge IGCSE and A-Level past papers and earlier benchmarks, with about 38% original, rewritten by contributors as Python templates (p.3-5, p.15). Solution steps were written in LaTeX with LLM help from the Python computation (p.15).
instances: generated: each template samples numbers, patterns, shapes, colours and function types and redraws the image (p.5, p.15-16); sampling uses a predetermined seed, so the 10 variants are reproducible (p.15-16).
has_gold_traces: yes: every instance carries template-generated step-by-step solutions in LaTeX alongside the computed answer (p.4, p.15).
evaluation: final answer, deterministic: numeric answers accepted within 1% of the ground truth, with worst-case accuracy over the 10 variants (p.5, p.24). Step-level, by LLM judge: GPT-5.4 decides whether each gold step is covered (recall) and whether each model step is valid against the gold solution (precision), giving F1 and a worst-case F1, on five models (p.6-7).
human_validation: Items: contributors cross-validated each other's templates (a contributor from another subject where only one worked on a subject), and a dedicated quality-control team checked the generated outputs, intermediate steps and final answers (p.4, p.16); no error counts are reported. Translations: native speakers verified the machine drafts, with deleted text planted in 40 of 606 descriptions as an attention check (p.4, p.16). Evaluator: none. The step judge is checked only by re-judging GPT-5.4's outputs with Gemini 2.5 Pro, where F1 shifts by +0.2 to -4.6 points (Table 13, p.24-25). 52 GPT-5.4 failures were inspected by hand (p.9).
contamination_measures: generated instances: variants across numbers, images and languages, framed as robustness 'beyond static benchmarks' (p.1, p.9). There is no private seed and no explicit contamination analysis.

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it. Sci-rho cites EngTrace's arXiv version (Gull et al., 2026, arXiv 2511.01650) together with FinChain (Xie et al., 2026) as the inspiration for its step precision and recall (p.6, references p.10, p.14). Its construction (expert-written Python templates that generate instances with computed answers and step-by-step solutions) is EngTrace's construction applied to visual school-level STEM.

suggested_wording: Sci-rho (Azmi et al., 2026) brings code templates to visually grounded school-level STEM in seven languages: 606 Python templates generate 42,420 instances with step-by-step solutions, final answers are checked within a 1% tolerance, and steps are judged against the gold solution by an LLM.
facts_to_cite: 606 templates in five school-level STEM subjects, written as Python classes by eight contributors including olympiad medalists (p.4-5, p.15)
Templates vary numbers, patterns, shapes, colours and function types, redraw the image, and generate step-by-step solutions with each instance (p.4-5, p.15-16)
Seven languages; 42,420 instances in total (10 variants x 606 templates x 7 languages) (p.1, p.5)
17 VLMs scored on average-case and worst-case accuracy over variants, with final answers matched within 1% tolerance and no model involved (p.5, p.24)
Closed models lose 10 to 28 points from average-case to worst-case accuracy (p.7)
Step precision, recall and F1 against the gold solution are judged by GPT-5.4, for five models (p.6-7)
The step judge is not validated against humans; robustness is checked by re-judging with Gemini 2.5 Pro (p.24-25)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: code templates that generate instances together with computed answers and gold step-by-step solutions (p.4, p.15), which is EngTrace's construction; deterministic final-answer checking against a tolerance (p.5); step-level evaluation against gold steps (p.6); robustness across generated variants (p.5-7); expert-written templates with peer cross-checks (p.4, p.16). Lacks: the engineering domain and university level (IGCSE and A-Level school science, p.3, p.5); deterministic step checks (steps are judged by an LLM); any human validation of the step evaluator (p.24-25); a private seed (variants come from a predetermined seed and the paper presents them as a robustness test, not a contamination defence); difficulty beyond two school levels. It adds what EngTrace lacks: images and multilinguality. What EngTrace adds beyond it: university-level engineering in five branches with three tiers, milestone and arithmetic checks that are deterministic rather than judged, a residual judge validated against 15 experts' step labels, and a private-seed pool.
notes: (1) '4,242 problem templates' in the abstract (p.1) counts each of the 606 templates once per language (606 x 7); the batch note's '4,242 expert-written Python templates' overstates the number of distinct templates, which is 606 (p.4-5). (2) Author-network overlap: Sci-rho's last author, Fajri Koto (MBZUAI, p.1), is a co-author of FinChain with several EngTrace authors (references, p.14), and Sci-rho adopts EngTrace's step precision and recall (p.6). The revised text must cite it in the third person without signalling the connection, and the authors should check whether ARR's conflict-of-interest rules are affected. (3) The search note's 'scored by worst-case accuracy across variants and step-level F1' is right, but step F1 is LLM-judged and covers only five models (p.7). (4) Placement: the physical-sciences paragraph, or the introduction's sentence on symbolic templates beside GSM-Symbolic and FinChain, not the engineering paragraph.
